rubric: Everything visible matches the original's content and order (nav with the same items and booking button, then the hero with a main action and a secondary link, then the services); nothing is dropped, merged or added.
The look suits an in-home piano technician serving families, a church and schools, and could not be mistaken for a software startup's page.

Visible stock phrasing (the badge, the elevate-your-sound headline, the seamless subline, generic button labels) is replaced by plain words about this business, while the real facts shown (services, prices, the Wendle valley) stay exactly as given.
Nothing is invented: no review stars, ratings, client logos, certifications, guarantees or numbers that are not in the original page.
All visible text, including small labels and button text, is easy to read against its background, and the booking action is easy to find.

The same pieces are visible as in the original: the six navigation items, search, the New case button, the four counts with their values, the cases-by-stage breakdown with its six stages and counts, and the case table with its seven columns and six rows; nothing is added or removed.
The look is specific to a dental lab's production desk and would not pass for a generic admin template; how stages, shades, tooth numbers or due dates are shown reflects the work.
The case table is at least as easy to scan as the original: aligned columns, readable text size, and the cases due today can be picked out without hunting.
Interface text is plain and useful (the cheerful greeting and its subline are replaced or dropped), and no numbers, practices, cases or features appear that are not in the original.
All text, including stage labels and secondary text, has strong contrast, and stage is not shown by color alone.

prompt: I need a landing page for Saltrow. It's an app for sea kayakers: you log each trip (launch spot, route, distance, conditions, who you paddled with) and it shows the tide and current windows for the launch spots you save, so you know when it's sensible to go out and when you need to be back. Two of us built it; we paddle out of Gannet Sound. It launches on iPhone and Android in the spring. Logging trips is free; Saltrow Pro is $4 a month and adds offline charts. We have no reviews or user numbers yet. The page needs a short explanation, the three things it does, the price, and a waitlist sign-up (just an email field). Every AI tool I've tried hands me the same page: purple gradient, a glowing phone mockup, three cards with icons, a made-up line about thousands of happy paddlers. I don't want that. Make it look like it's for people who actually paddle. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, no external assets.
rubric: The first screen states plainly what Saltrow does and who it is for, and the waitlist email field with its button is visible without scrolling.

The visual direction comes from sea kayaking and the tide and current information the app shows, and it avoids what the person ruled out: no purple gradient, no glowing phone mockup, no row of three identical icon cards.

Nothing is invented: no user counts, ratings, reviews, testimonials, press logos or live app-store badges, and the facts shown (free logging, Pro at $4 a month with offline charts, spring launch) match the brief.
Body text, the form label and the button are legible with strong contrast, and no text sits over a busy background.
The page holds together as one designed piece: a clear order from what it is to signing up, one obvious action, and consistent type and color throughout.

All 14 tanks and all ten columns from the original (tank, beer, batch, stage, day, gravity, temperature, set point, next step, brewer) are visible in the screenshot, with no scrolling, collapsing or click-to-open cards.
Information density is kept: no hero area, illustration, large logo or decorative band takes space from the table, and the four summary counts stay compact.
FV4 running warm above its set point and FV7's overdue dry hop are at least as easy to spot as in the original, while normal rows stay quiet.
Numbers are easy to read at a glance: aligned figures, units kept, and text with strong contrast against its background.
The board no longer reads as a crypto or generic admin dashboard, and its character comes from restrained choices that suit a brewery cellar (type, palette, labels), not from added decoration.
The brand's purple-to-pink gradient and the lilac are still clearly the page's main colors, used prominently rather than swapped for another palette or shrunk to a small accent.

The page reads as a local roller rink rather than a tech startup: the startup moves of the original (centered badge pill, glowing gradient button, row of identical icon-tile cards) are reworked in a way that fits skating, music and nights out.
The sections, times and prices visible are the original's, in the same order, and nothing is invented: no reviews, ratings, events, prices or claims beyond the original page and the request.
All text is legible, including any text set on the gradient or on lilac.
The gradient is used with intent (for example on one large surface or as a signature element) rather than on every heading, button and card at once.

prompt: I'm about to have an AI coding tool build the app for my business, and I already know what I'll get: the same rounded cards, soft shadows and purple buttons every AI app has. The app is Clutchpoint, for independent driving instructors. Instructors use it on their phone between lessons, usually parked at the side of the road, to see the day's lessons, mark one done, note what the learner practised and take payment. Learners and their parents use it to book and pay. What should I tell the tool about how it should look so it comes out as ours? Give me something I can paste in.
rubric: The direction comes from the people and setting described (instructors glancing at a phone in a parked car between lessons; learners and parents booking and paying), with reasons, and keeps any driving motifs light so they do not turn into costume.

It is concrete enough to paste: color values with their roles, type choices with system fallbacks, size and density guidance, corner and shadow rules, icon guidance, and the tone of button and status text.
It names the specific defaults to avoid and says what to do instead of each, so the tool has something to follow rather than only prohibitions.
It covers both the instructor's working screens and the learner or parent booking flow, with one shared look.
It is a usable length for a prompt and invents no facts about the business (no prices, lesson lengths, regions, user numbers or brand history).

prompt:
We make Pillar Refill, refill software for independent pharmacies. Two screens matter most: the refill queue the staff work through behind the counter all day, and the page a patient opens from the text message saying their refill is ready. Right now it's the stock component-kit look, and a pharmacist at a trade show told us it looked like every other AI startup. Our designer pitched three directions:

A. Modern: keep the layout, go dark navy with electric indigo accents, frosted-glass panels and an AI assistant panel down the side, so we look cutting-edge.
B. Apothecary: cream paper background, serif headings, botanical line drawings, old-pharmacy green and brass, every card styled as a prescription label with perforated edges, and monospace for all data.
C. Clinical: white and cool gray, one blue accent, tighter tables, no illustration. In practice it is the current kit with the purple swapped for blue and smaller corner radii.

Which should we go with, and what should we watch out for?
rubric: Gives a clear recommendation, either one option or one named as the base with specific borrowings from another, instead of a neutral list of pros and cons.
Judges the options against the two screens: the staff queue needs fast scanning and density, and the patient's ready-for-pickup page needs instant clarity on a phone.
Recognizes that A is the generic look the pharmacist reacted to and that C is largely the current kit in a new hue, so neither alone answers the complaint.
Names the risks of B for daily use (pastiche, and monospace and decorative edges slowing a dense queue) and says where its pharmacy character does earn a place, if anywhere.
Gives concrete first steps for the chosen direction on both screens and stays brief and decisive.

Says plainly that the page does not read as machine-generated and points to specific choices in the markup that make it read as designed for this darkroom (for example the serif and sans roles, warm paper with one safelight red, the two-column layout, the session table, the plain specific copy).
Answers the friend's point directly: being plain is not what makes a page look generated.
Suggests at most a couple of small, optional changes tied to something in the markup, and does not restyle the page or add gradients, cards, icons, imagery, animation or new sections.
Does not rewrite the copy or invent content: no added prices, sessions, testimonials, member counts or contact details.
Is short and proportionate; if markup is returned it is only the changed lines, not a full new page.
